items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models

By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: Vue Customer Reports: Node Grants, Private Objects, Axios Upload Metering
items.summary: Customer support reports have an awkward boundary: the browser should move bytes quickly, but it should never decide where a customer's file lives. Short answer: let a Node backend authorize a tenant-scoped key and presigned upload URL, let Vue/Axios upload directly with progress events, then issue a short-lived signed read URL only when an authenticated customer asks for the report. That split keeps credentials and naming policy on the server while avoiding a second hop for the file itself. It also gives the UI an honest progress bar instead of pretending that a completed POST means the object is durable. The tempting implementation is a browser POST to your Node server, followed by a server-side upload. It is easy to explain, and it is expensive in operational terms: your API process becomes a byte pump, request timeouts become file-size limits, and a support agent watching a report upload competes with ordinary API traffic. The direct pattern has three explicit steps. First, the authenticated request asks Node for a key and a presigned URL. items.title: Cache-Busting Static Assets with ?v=: So Visitors Actually Get the Fix
items.summary: The most embarrassing bug report I ever got went like this: I fixed a bug, deployed it, tested it myself, and the visitor still saw the broken version. The new file was on the server. My own browser showed the fix. Then I talked the visitor through clearing their cache, and suddenly everything worked. The bug was never in my code. It was in the browser cache, and it taught me the cheapest lesson in web performance: browsers remember your files far longer than you expect, and you have to give them a reason to forget. When a browser downloads style.css or app.js, it keeps a copy. The next time it needs that file, it checks its cache first. If the server sent a far-future Cache-Control header like max-age=31536000, the browser may not even ask the server whether the file changed. It just serves the old copy, silently, for a year. That is exactly what you want for performance. A returning visitor should not re-download files that have not changed. The problem starts the day you do change one. The URL is identical, the filename is identical, and the browser has no way of knowing the contents are different. Your fix is live on the server and invisible to everyone who visited before. ?v=

So a router can give each route its own screen through the id: "/items/:itemId": (p) => ( ), Going from item 1 to item 2 changes only the id, so React keeps the element. UECA kept its model too and renamed it: no init, and item 2 opened with item 1's state. It turned up while checking the shipped agent skills against 3.2.1, whose scaffold router had exactly this shape. Now the id is the element's key. A new id gets its own model, and the old one waits in the cache until its id comes back. editor: useNestedEditor({ data: UECA.bind(() => model.entity, "nested"), }), The owner and the child share one object, so the child's edits land in the entity. When the owner reloaded the entity and the nested object came back equal but as a new instance, UECA treated it as no change. items.title: How Cursive Text Generators Work: Unicode, Not Fonts
items.summary: If you have ever pasted fancy script text into a bio and wondered why it works without installing a font, the answer is Unicode. This short explainer covers how a cursive font generator turns normal letters into script-looking characters, and what to watch out for. A font changes how characters are drawn. Cursive text generators do something different: they swap each letter for a different Unicode code point that already looks like script. For example, the letter "a" can map to a mathematical script character. The result is plain text, so it survives copy and paste. const map = { a: "𝒶", b: "𝒷", c: "𝒸" }; const toScript = (s) => [...s].map((ch) => map[ch] ?? ch).join(""); A real tool covers upper and lower case, and handles letters that have no script version by leaving them unchanged. Accessibility: screen readers may read each symbol by its long Unicode name, so keep key information in plain text. Search: styled characters are not matched by normal search, so do not style anything you want people to find. Support: very old devices can show empty boxes for rare symbols. items.title: Zustand: React State Without the Boilerplate
items.summary: Picture a small shop page with a cart icon in the corner. A visitor adds a tote bag and a mug. Three parts of the page need to know what happened: the cart icon showing the count, the cart drawer listing the items, and the checkout button showing the total. If each part keeps its own copy of the cart, the numbers drift apart. The usual fix is to lift the state up to a shared parent, but that turns every middle component into a courier for data it never uses. That is the problem Zustand sets out to solve, and the question is whether a tiny store does the job better than the tools React already ships with. My first check is how much state needs sharing. One cart icon and one list on the same page can live in a parent component, and a library buys nothing there. Once three or more distant parts read the same state, or it must survive a route change, a shared store earns its keep. Count the readers first. My second check is the learning curve, and Zustand is light here. A store is a function call with state fields plus the functions that change them. No provider, no reducer, no action types. On a phone connection, a 200 MB video can become nearly impossible to send. Chunked uploading fixes this with a simple idea: cut the file into pieces, send the pieces one by one, and let the server put them back together. If the connection dies, you only resend the pieces the server never got. The browser slices the file with Blob.slice() — no plugin, no library needed. Each chunk is sent with three pieces of information: an upload ID, the chunk index, and the total chunk count. The server stores the chunks under that upload ID. items.summary: Crash games are one of the simplest games of chance you can model in code. A multiplier starts at 1.00x and climbs until it "crashes" at a random point. Players cash out before the crash to win their stake × the multiplier, or lose it if they wait too long. Aviator, JetX and Spaceman all work this way. Because the rules are so simple, they're a great playground for Monte Carlo simulation. They also attract a huge amount of nonsense: "predictor" apps, Telegram "signal" groups and betting systems that promise to beat the game. So we built a seeded simulator, ran 10 million rounds, and tested the most popular strategies. Here's how it works, with code you can run. Most valuation methods start from your forecasts and end at a price: guess growth, margins and a discount rate, then compute what the company is "worth". items.title: Implementing Node.js Backpressure for Daily Report Emails (Public HTTPS Push)
items.summary: Short answer: start the daily report with cron, publish one idempotent job per delivery, and let a bounded worker pool enforce the email provider's rate limit; choose push only when a public HTTPS subscriber is an acceptable security boundary. For a healthtech team, the useful optimization target isn't raw send speed. It is controlled recovery: after a provider returns 429, the backlog must remain identifiable, duplicate-safe, and able to drain without turning the next day's report into a second traffic spike. A cron handler that also sends every email hides those states inside one long invocation. The cron-to-queue split makes them operable. Infrai is one option I would test when setup time is the constraint. Its public discovery surface exposes the request schema, response schema, billing metadata, and runnable examples for each capability without requiring a key, so checking a scheduling contract is an HTTP read rather than an SDK evaluation. Infrai uses one API key across all capabilities and consolidates their usage on one bill. items.title: Loading 100 Photos from PHPicker Without Freezing: Order, Progress and Cancellation in Swift
items.summary: Someone selects 80 photos in the system picker, taps Add, and your app goes quiet. No spinner, no count, just a frozen sheet while the item providers grind through iCloud downloads in whatever order they finish. When the results finally arrive, photo 37 is in slot 2, two files are missing, and nobody knows why. PHPickerViewController is the right tool for picking photos on iOS: no full library permission, the system handles the UI, and it supports multi-select. But the part after picker(_:didFinishPicking:) is all yours, and that is where batch apps tend to go wrong. This post covers the loading side: keeping the user's order, copying files before they vanish, limiting concurrency, showing honest progress, and letting people cancel. items.title: How to revoke Sign in with Apple tokens when deleting a Supabase account
items.summary: If your iOS app offers Sign in with Apple, Apple asks you to revoke the person's token when they delete their account. With Supabase that's awkward: native sign-in uses signInWithIdToken, so you never receive an Apple refresh token, and at deletion time you have nothing to revoke. Here's an approach that works without storing anything from Apple. When the person taps Delete Account, show the Sign in with Apple sheet once more. It returns a fresh authorization code, valid for five minutes and usable once. Send that code to a Supabase Edge Function. The function exchanges the code for a refresh token at https://appleid.apple.com/auth/token. It revokes that token at https://appleid.apple.com/auth/revoke. Only then does it delete the Supabase user. A Sign in with Apple key (.p8) from Certificates, Identifiers & Profiles > Keys, plus its Key ID and your Team ID. Those stored as Edge Function secrets, never in the app. A client secret for each request: a short-lived JWT signed with the key using ES256. items.title: Stop Guessing Which Bit Changed. .NET 11 Prints Doubles in Hex
items.summary: TL;DR: In .NET 11, double, float, and Half accept the "X" format and NumberStyles.HexFloat. You get the exact bits as readable text, like 0x1.3333333333334p-2, and you can parse them straight back. This ships in .NET 11, which went GA on 2026-11-10. Everything below was run on the .NET 11 RC 1 SDK. Every .NET developer meets this pair of lines sooner or later: double sum = 0.1 + 0.2; Console.WriteLine(sum); // 0.30000000000000004 Console.WriteLine(sum == 0.3); // False So how far off is it? Decimal text cannot really tell you. It shows you a long tail of digits and leaves the counting to you. The old way to see the truth was to dump the raw bits: Console.WriteLine(BitConverter.DoubleToInt64Bits(sum).ToString("X16")); // 3FD3333333333334 Console.WriteLine(BitConverter.DoubleToInt64Bits(0.3).ToString("X16")); // 3FD3333333333333 That works if you enjoy decoding sign, exponent, and mantissa by hand. It is technically readable, the way a tax form is technically readable. Two things, one for each direction: The "X" and "x" format specifiers now work on double, float, and Half, and produce the IEEE 754 hexadecimal form. items.summary: Most of the "my Lovable app won't deploy" messages I see come down to one of a handful of causes. Some are inside Lovable (the change was never published, the build failed, a security scan or a workspace policy blocked it). The rest happen when you move the app to Vercel, Netlify or Cloudflare and the host is set up for the wrong kind of build. Here is how I find which one it is, and the fix for each. Publishing failed Fix security issues to publish Publishing is blocked by workspace policy You don't have permission to publish this project Or no message at all: the deploy on Vercel or Netlify fails, or the live site still shows old changes. A small dot on the Publish button means there are unpublished changes. The build fails. An error in the code stops the deploy. items.title: Build in stages
items.summary: After version 4 of the specification was approved, I did not open a editor and start on the home page. I built in the order the specification named. Five stages are in the running site. Payments are not. That is a choice, not a delay I forgot about. A profile photo needs a file store. A group home page needs a page editor, and the page editor needs a sanitizer. A class you can sell needs the class to exist. If I build checkout first, I am designing a cash register for a store with no shelves. Each stage has a gate. The code for a later stage does not start because I am excited about it. The specification says which stage a feature waits on. I followed that. Stage 1. Poe, per group. A member's bot key is not one key for the whole site. It belongs to a group. The owner can require a member's own key, set a monthly cap, and limit which bots that member may use. The public Poe catalog does not list private prompt bots. I wrote that limit into the screen instead of pretending the API returns them. Stage 2. Documents. Logos, profile photos, and member files are rows, not paths pasted into a form. Images are resized. items.title: I built a native Mac Markdown editor solo, with zero dependencies. It launched on Product Hunt today
items.summary: Hi DEV! I'm Pedro, and for the past months I've been building Coffee, a Markdown editor for the Mac, on my own. It went live on Product Hunt today, so here's what it is and a few things I learned building it. What it does Plain files. Every note is a .md file in a folder you choose. No database for your writing, no import step, and any other editor can open the same folder (an Obsidian vault works as it is). Answers beside the line. Write 20% of 50, $30 in EUR, Tokyo time or half of 175 and the answer appears next to the line, without going into your file. Maths and Mermaid, drawn natively. No web view: TeX and Mermaid diagrams are rendered by the app itself. Review every AI edit. When Claude, Cursor or anything else changes a note's file, Coffee lays out every change and you keep or undo each one. MCP, off by default. AI apps can read and write your notes over MCP, but only once you turn it on. Swift 6.2 and SwiftPM, macOS 15 and later. Zero third-party dependencies. The Markdown parser, the Mermaid and TeX renderers and the calculator are all written for the app. Search runs on the system's SQLite. items.title: Day 18: The Error Contract and User Visible Messages
items.summary: A failed call comes in two kinds. One is a business rule stopping something in the normal course of things, an order with no customer selected, a status that cannot move that way, and that message is written for the user. The other is an exception the code did not expect, whose message may carry a file path from the server, and that one is written for the developer. Both look identical by the time they reach the caller, both being the error field in a JSON-RPC payload. Without telling them apart the only safe thing to display is "request failed", and the half the user was supposed to see goes with it. Telling them apart means that field needs a contract of its own. items.title: React error #418: fixing a matchMedia hydration mismatch with useSyncExternalStore
items.summary: Minified React error #418 means the HTML the server rendered did not match what the client rendered on its first pass. On my Next.js site the cause was a useMediaQuery hook that read window.matchMedia(query).matches inside a useState initializer. The server returned false, a desktop browser returned true, and React threw away the server HTML. Rewriting the hook on useSyncExternalStore with a getServerSnapshot of false made the first client render match the server by construction. React 19 reports it as "Hydration failed because the server rendered HTML didn't match the client." During hydration React walks the server HTML and the first client render side by side. If one has a node the other lacks, React cannot reuse the markup. It discards the server tree and renders the whole app again on the client. In production the message is minified, so all you get is #418 and a link. It names no component and no node. On my site it fired on every production page load, and nothing looked broken, because the client re-render produced a correct page. The cost was invisible: the server HTML was thrown away, and every visitor paid for a full client render. I think this is what my earlier performa

items.title: Next.js soft 404: why notFound() returned 200 behind loading.tsx
items.summary: On my Next.js 16 site, a URL like /projects/nope returned HTTP 200 and carried two robots tags: index, follow and noindex. The route has a loading.tsx, which starts streaming before notFound() runs, so the status code was already sent. Adding export const dynamicParams = false to the page makes an unknown slug a real 404 before any rendering starts. I found this during a Search Console pass. Unknown project slugs were not 404s. The Next.js docs describe the mechanism in the loading.js reference: streaming page responses begin with a 200 status code, and the initial response headers fix the status for the rest of the response. Next.js can still stream notFound() after that, so the browser shows your not-found UI, but the status line stays 200. The docs also say when the stream starts. The response body begins streaming when a Suspense fallback renders, and they give loading.tsx as the example, or when a Server Component suspends under a boundary. Calling notFound() before that point preserves the 404. After it, the status cannot change. A loading.tsx file is a Suspense fallback wrapped around the segment's page. items.title: Next.js metadata openGraph not inherited: why my subpages lost og:site_name
items.summary: If a page in the Next.js App Router sets its own openGraph, the openGraph object from your layout is gone for that page. Next.js merges metadata shallowly, so og:site_name, og:locale and any other field you only set in the layout disappear. The fix I use is one helper that builds the full openGraph and twitter objects for every subpage, plus a build check that fails when a tag is missing. I found this on my own site, mohamedgado.com. /now, /projects and all 55 case studies were shipping without og:site_name, og:locale, twitter:site and twitter:creator. The root layout set all four. Nothing in the browser looked wrong, and nothing errored. No, not field by field. The Next.js 16 docs for generateMetadata say that metadata objects exported from several segments of one route are shallowly merged, and that duplicate keys are replaced by the segment closest to the page. They also say it directly for nested fields: openGraph defined in an earlier segment is overwritten by the last segment that defines it. The docs give the example. items.title: React Query Showed the Wrong User's Data — Here's How to Reproduce and Fix It
items.summary: A React dashboard can display the wrong user's data even when the API is returning the correct response. One of the easiest ways to introduce this bug is by using a query key that doesn't account for the current user. Consider this: const { data } = useQuery({ queryKey: ["orders"], queryFn: () => fetchOrders(userId), }); It looks perfectly reasonable. But there's a problem. The query function depends on userId, while the cache key doesn't. If Alice's orders are already cached and the application switches to Bob, both users can end up sharing the same cache entry. Depending on the query's freshness settings, Bob's dashboard could display Alice's previously cached orders. I wanted to break down why this happens because it's the kind of issue that's easy to overlook when testing with only one account. We'll reproduce it in a small React application, fix the query key, and then look at what changes when authentication, logout, and multiple SaaS workspaces are involved. items.title: Snapping a tap to a real corner: building a LiDAR tape measure for iPhone
items.summary: When you tap the screen to start a measurement, you are not tapping the corner of the table. You are tapping a pixel, and that pixel sits on a ray that leaves the camera and hits something. Often the something is the floor 40 inches behind the table, because your thumb landed a hair past the edge. This post is how the tape measure in our iPhone app deals with that: two kinds of evidence (depth and image), a little geometry, and a filter that refuses to let the point jitter. On a Pro iPhone, ARKit hands you a depth map with every frame (sceneDepth, plus smoothedSceneDepth when the device supports it) and a confidence map next to it. It is wonderful and it is coarse. The reconstructed mesh is a few centimetres per triangle, so it rounds off exactly the thing you want to measure to: the edge. It is also blind to edges that are flat on a surface. A picture frame on a wall, door trim, the printed edge of a box: depth sees one plane. The camera image sees a sharp line. So the snapper looks at both, every frame, in a small window around the reticle. items.summary: In 2004, as a university student, I wrote a physics lab in Delphi 7 and OpenGL for use in lessons. If you’d told me that one day I’d use the same desktop platform to trace light around a black hole and referee a game of eight-ball, I’d have wanted to see the code. The original lab is still there. Browse the Delphi source on GitHub Today I build Makarov Suites in Munich. Physics, Math and Astronomy are on Steam for Windows. Engineering, Earth and Games are in development. Here are all six in 35 seconds, recorded directly from the applications. Makarov Physics Suite Watch the last shot of the Physics reel. A wave travels along a row of coloured pendulums, yet each bob swings in its own plane. They have slightly different lengths, so each one gains a little on its neighbour. The wave is what you see when you follow the whole row. The reel starts inside a tokamak, then follows the rods on a steam locomotive and the grains in a rotating drum. The drum is a good first experiment to try yourself. Let it get up to speed, then reverse the motor. The drive changes direction while the grains still carry momentum from a moment ago. items.title: Test your Polly retry policy against a real failing server
items.summary: Most retry policies are tested in one of two ways: not at all, or with a mocked HttpMessageHandler that throws on cue. The mock proves that Polly calls your delegate again. It doesn't show what your app does when a real server is slow, answers 503 twice, then takes three seconds to say yes. Here's a way to see that in about five minutes, with no change to your app except the URL. I built Curler for this. You create a bin, give it a script of responses, and point your app at the bin's URL. Every call your app makes shows up with the response Curler sent, when it was sent and how long it took. The script for this post: { "steps": [ { "status": 503, "times": 2 }, { "status": 200, "delayMs": 3000, "contentType": "application/json", "body": "{\"paid\":true}" } ] } Two 503s, then a 200 that takes three seconds. The last step repeats, so every call after the second gets the slow success. This is a payment provider on a bad day. To use it: open curler.dev, click Create a bin, click Edit in the Responses bar, paste the script and save. Copy the capture URL from the top bar. A console app with Polly v8. items.title: New York Launches Nation's First State AI Testing Program
items.summary: New York is launching a state-backed AI safety research center at Binghamton University that will independently study and test AI systems, develop safety and security techniques, and train researchers in responsible AI. "While the federal government fails to act, New York is leading the way on AI safety and holding big tech accountable," New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said. "The stakes are too high to simply take AI companies at their word." Politico reports: The center -- which is funded by a $30 million gift from Bloomberg co-founder Tom Secunda and a $25 million research investment from SUNY and New York state -- is set to launch before New York's major AI safety law, the RAISE Act, comes into effect on Jan. 1. That will require submissions of detailed safety frameworks from AI companies operating in New York State, which Hochul's office hopes will be scrutinized by researchers at the new center. "AI is opening up questions that scientists could not tackle before," said Secunda, who also serves as the board chair of Empire AI, a $500 million public-private partnership. items.title: React Page Missing From Google? Three Checks Before You Rewrite It
items.summary: A React page can work in your browser while its initial HTTP response contains only an app shell. That observation alone does not prove Google cannot index it. Separate three questions: what did the server return, what could Google render, and what version is currently indexed? Pick a service or article URL with a unique heading. Save its response: curl -sSL -D headers.txt -o page.html https://example.com/services/web-development Check the status, robots directives, canonical URL and main content. Compare it with the homepage. Also test a URL that should not exist: an error screen returning HTTP 200 can create a soft-404 problem. Use Search Console’s URL Inspection live test. Search the tested HTML for a sentence unique to the page. If it is absent, investigate failed scripts, data requests and content that depends on clicking a button. A loader in a screenshot is a useful clue, but inspect the HTML too. Google documents the distinction between crawling, rendering and indexing in its JavaScript SEO guide. items.title: What I learned building an auto-tiling window manager for macOS with the Accessibility API
items.summary: Snug is a menu bar app that tiles every window the moment it opens. Open a window and it drops into the next free tile; close one and the rest reflow with no holes. There's no config file, and it never asks for Screen Recording permission: it reads each window's position, size and owning app, and nothing else. macOS has no window manager API, so everything goes through the Accessibility API (AXUIElement). Here's what that taught me. Each AX call is a synchronous message to another app, so a busy or hung app can stall the caller. Snug runs one background thread that owns every AX call, every observer and the tiler's state. The main thread only draws UI. A detail worth knowing: a thread's run loop exits immediately if it has no sources, so the AX thread adds a dummy port to keep it alive before any observer exists. RunLoop.current.add(NSMachPort(), forMode: .default) // keeps the run loop alive with no sources There's an AXObserver per running app, listening for window created, moved, resized, minimized and restored, focus changes, and the app hiding or showing. items.title: How I built auto-zoom for screen recordings that you can actually edit (Swift + ScreenCaptureKit)
items.summary: I make small Mac apps you buy once. The newest is MacMuse Recorder, a screen recorder whose main feature is automatic zoom: you click around while recording, and the finished video pushes in on the part that matters. Screen Studio made that look popular. What I wanted on top of it was control: every zoom should be an ordinary block on the timeline, so when the guess is wrong you drag it, retime it or delete it instead of fighting it. This post is how that works under the hood. Everything is Swift on macOS 15+, and the snippets are the real code. While ScreenCaptureKit writes the video, the app keeps three other streams: Cursor samples. Clicks, from an NSEvent global monitor for mouse-down events. Activity. ScreenCaptureKit attaches dirty rects to each frame: the regions that changed since the last one. I boil them down to about 10 samples a second, each a bounding box plus the fraction of the screen that changed. struct Activity: Codable, Equatable { var t: Double, x0: Double, y0: Double, x1: Double, y1: Double, a: Double } Activity is what lets a zoom follow typing, menus and dialogs, not just clicks. items.title: Two SwiftUI animation loops that burned CPU on my Mac with nothing on screen
items.summary: A looping animation looks free. On macOS, two of mine were not. Both shipped in my own apps, and both were measured on release builds, not Debug. Soluna is my menu bar calendar. Today’s cell had a slow “breathing” glow, a .repeatForever animation on one flag. My own Mac health app, What Happened, reported Soluna using about 134 core-minutes a day in the background. The cause: AppKit keeps an NSPopover’s hosting view alive between opens. So after the popover closed, SwiftUI went on re-rendering its whole view tree every frame. sample showed the main thread in NSHostingView.layout and ViewGraphRootValueUpdater.render with nothing on screen. I proved it by toggling. Open and close the popover: 17 to 19% of a core, and it stays. Close it on a month that does not contain today’s cell: 0.0%. Back to today: 17% again. The rule I took from it: any looping animation inside a popover or panel has to stop when it closes. Wick is my deadline tracker, and a deadline can show a small flame. Each flame was a TimelineView(.animation) drawing into a Canvas. With the window in front and idle, the app sat at 32% of a core. With flame motion off: 0%. A single flame: about 12%. Blender 5.3 also brings support for NVIDIA RTX Spark devices. For the Cycles code in Blender 5.3 the Principled BSDF for shader nodes now supports dispersion. Another notable change with Blender 5.3 is the Vulkan back-end now being the default on Windows (except for Windows on ARM) and Linux systems. Vulkan 1.1 or newer is required and should deliver better performance than OpenGL. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.summary: Our Family Album is a private photo album for families. Parents post a moment once, and the people they invited see it right away. It launched in July 2026. And the main engineering problem turned out to be one sentence I kept hearing from users: "My parents won't install another app." 😅 Version 1.5 added Share without an app. From the invitation screen or an album's menu you can do two things: Create a browser link for one person. It opens the album read-only on any device, with no account. Each link is made for a single person, can expire after 30 days, and can be revoked at any time. Invite someone by email. Each photo email includes a link to the full album, so relatives can catch up from their inbox. Browser access is read-only on purpose. Uploading, commenting and reacting stay inside the app, where people have accounts. The first versions stored some album settings in UserDefaults on the device. That breaks as soon as two family members change settings on two different phones. So now: Album permissions come from the server, not from local storage. A save waits for the server to confirm it. items.summary: Geo Adventures is a geography game: you're dropped into a real street view somewhere in the world, you look for clues, and you pin your guess on a map. It launched in August 2026. It's built with plain UIKit and Auto Layout in code. The challenge was making it not feel like UIKit at all 🎮 Games don't have navigation bars and standard alerts, so I built my own: GameButton: chunky 3D "arcade pill" buttons with a pressed state. GameHeaderView instead of UINavigationBar. GameAlertController instead of UIAlertController. SpringModalTransition for bouncy modal presentations. A starfield background, confetti, Core Haptics patterns and system sounds for feedback. A ThemeManager (the same pattern I use in Email Me) switches between four themes: Midnight, Ocean, Sunset and Daylight. Google Maps SDK shows the Street View panoramas. MapKit handles the guess map and the result map, so those screens don't need a Google key. You can play right away as a guest, even offline. items.summary: Photo Booth App turns an iPhone or iPad into a self-service photo booth for weddings, parties and company events. Version 1.0 went live in March 2026, and I've shipped more than 20 updates since. An event app doesn't forgive mistakes: if a photo gets lost at a wedding, there's no retake next week. Venue Wi-Fi is usually bad, so the booth never depends on it: Photos and GIFs are captured and saved on the device first. Uploads to the online gallery run in the background and keep going while guests keep using the booth. Finished photos survive the booth restarting or moving on to the next guest. When an event opens, the app checks the gallery and recovers any saved photos that are missing. Sharing by QR code, email or text needs a connection. Taking photos never does. AirPrint is easy to add and hard to get right: A 4×6 template used to print in the corner of a full sheet 🤦 Now the paper size is matched to the template size. items.title: One photo frame codebase for iPhone, iPad, Mac and Apple TV, back to iOS 12
items.summary: Digital Photo Frame turns an Apple device into a picture frame. It's been on the App Store since March 2017, and it has shipped more than 160 releases. The interesting engineering isn't the slideshow itself. It's keeping it running, alone, for weeks. The app is one Xcode project with an iOS target, a Mac Catalyst build, a tvOS target and a WidgetKit extension. It's UIKit, with MVVM for the main screens, coordinators for navigation, and a service layer for every photo source: Apple Photos and iCloud shared albums Google Photos Self-hosted servers through Immich or WebDAV/NAS Flickr and Unsplash On the Mac, a small AppKit plugin bundle covers what Catalyst can't do. The deployment target is still iOS 12. A lot of people run the app on an old iPad that can't update anymore, and that's exactly the point of the product. The cost shows up in the dependencies. RevenueCat 5 needs iOS 13, so I vendor a patched copy of RevenueCat 4.43.4 inside the repo instead of pulling it through Swift Package Manager. Not pretty, but it works. Further trials in larger animal models are required before human testing can begin.

items.title: Microsoft Took 31 Years to Let You Kill Windows 11's Sticky Keys Popup
items.summary: Microsoft is testing a Windows 11 option that lets users permanently disable the Sticky Keys and Filter Keys activation prompts directly from the pop-ups themselves, ending a 31-year-old annoyance without requiring a trip into Settings. Windows Latest reports: Sadly, the dialog is still the same aging Win32 window, but we spotted Microsoft's design boss replying under an X post reply about this, saying he is working on modernizing legacy dialogs. The popup might be annoying, but did you know that it exists because of a pinball game from 1995? [...] The change is in Build 26340.9882 (Experimental) and Build 26320.9876 (Beta), both released on November 6 and based on Windows 11 version 26H2. Microsoft says you can "choose not to be asked again" from the Sticky Keys and Filter Keys dialogs, but it's a Controlled Feature Rollout in Experimental, so you may not see it yet. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

"I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape," Trump said at a White House briefing. The Associated Press reports: Trump suggested the extraordinary step of directly involving himself in a counterintelligence investigation, a sign of his friendly relationship with Huang and the possible geopolitical stakes. "I did speak to him today just to see if he's feeling all right, how you're doing," Trump said. "He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy." Trump is slated to meet next week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, but he was noncommittal about bringing up the situation with Xi. "No, I don't think so," Trump said. "I mean, maybe. I'm sure President XI will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he's a very honorable man." items.title: Crime pays: how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus
items.summary: Ever since it crashed on to PC and consoles in the late 90s, GTA has been tearing up the game-making rulebook. They would be ushered one by one into a darkened room to sit facing an enormous TV. The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways. SpudCell could potentially be misused, so its researchers are taking security seriously from the start - its DNA and proteins are engineered so that it can only survive on an exotic diet of chemicals not found in nature.

items.title: ‘There is no inevitable dystopia’: Jeanette Winterson on AI and the future of humanity
items.summary: The author believes we are at a turning point as a species – and even in the shadow of big tech it’s up to us how we want to proceed ‘I am a storyteller by trade,” writes Jeanette Winterson on the first page of her 2021 book 12 Bytes, an idiosyncratic and thought-provoking series of essays in which she considered just how artificial intelligence might change everything about our lives. “And I know everything we do is a fiction until it’s a fact: the dream of flying, the dream of space travel, the dream of speaking to someone instantly, across time and space, the dream of not dying – or of returning.” She had already been thinking about our possible futures for at least 15 years – her 2007 novel, The Stone Gods, for instance, imagined a post-climate catastrophe world populated by robots and humans who never age, while 12 Bytes was preceded by Frankisstein: A Love Story, which alternates a recreation of the summer Mary Shelley wrote Frankenstein with a trans doctor’s travels among present-day cryogenecists and AI-enabled robots.
